It is important that everyone read this with an open mind and think it through.

This will be long, it's necessary to examine the how and why of a change like this carefully.

Ask yourself this... why does a sub with 1000 subscribers self-moderate near-flawlessly using nothing but the most basic up/down voting system... while a sub with over 250k subscribers inevitably become a cesspool of group infighting, recycled content, and lowest common denominator trash? Why can't we maintain the quality of the original, smaller sub as it grows without resorting to power moderators, complex rules, and bots - which eventually create their own problems?

Well, what's the real difference between these two places?

When the sub starts, it is small and invisible, only attracting subscribers that actively search it out. The people subscribing in the youth of the sub are the people with a direct interest in that sub's topic matter. The sub will quickly develop a culture and a common behavior through discussions with other members. These original members are the people who make the place interesting enough to start attracting more new users.

As the sub grows, however... (1k to 250k)

  • the rate of submissions rises quickly (5 a day vs 200 a day)
  • more new users find it each day - users who don't know the sub's culture and do not care
  • the ratio of moderators to subscribers goes way out of balance (500 to 1 vs 125,000 to 1)
  • old mods are tired, vastly more mod work is required leading to burnout or laziness
  • new mods are less keen on the subject than old mods who created the place, good mods hard to find
  • cliques of users formed that want different things, they fight with each other over what's on or off topic
  • spammers are drawn in by the popularity and begin aggressively self-promoting crap content
  • bursts of new users and drive-by voting is caused by every post hitting high on /all
  • links to the sub are shared in high profile subs like askreddit causing the same
  • content quality degrades, driving away more discerning contributors and original members

We've all seen this play out on reddit a couple thousand times. Frankly, I don't think this problem can be solved by traditional human moderation. If Voat duplicates reddit, then Voat will become reddit. We have to try something different.

Having a mod 'team' attracts the wrong kind of people who stay for the wrong reasons, and over time the team quality degrades. I know of precious few moderation teams that have managed to dodge this bullet, and the few that did, tend to have subs that have an incredibly narrow topic focus. It's much harder to argue about what's on topic when you have a narrow focus, so people get behind the ideas of a narrow focus sub with more solidarity.

The solution is to find a way to somehow, organically, turn those original 1000 people into moderators by the time that crowd of 250k people has shown up. This is a different kind of moderation, where the oldest community members quietly acquire distributed power. The key question here is, how do we grant them greater power, and how do we keep it distributed fairly enough that the power comes from the aggregate in a democratic fashion, rather than from a chosen few?

It's incredibly simple to implement, really... all you have to do is make sure that the votes of the original subscribers count more than the new arrivals. This is the point where some of you are going to have a negative knee-jerk reaction to this idea. I'd urge you to think twice. There are many ways to do this, and being critical of the general idea is not the same as being critical of a specific implementation.

Know that this is playing with fire. Make the votes too heavy, and you will create power user cliques and turn every subverse into an echo chamber that buries new ideas. That was part of digg's problem. Make the votes too light, and you'll end up with reddit's problem, where all uniqueness and quality is washed away by a sea of lazy new users crashing the party.

There must be a balance between these two extremes. On striking that balance, the voting system itself should be sufficient to handle almost all moderation - turning the actual moderators into people who merely need tend to the CSS, or set a few dials and fiddles on subverse options. The mods won't need to police content any longer because thousands of subscribers are empowered to do that job.

I think the number one most important thing we can do for the long term health of this website is to experiment until we find that balance. This is as democratic as moderation can be, drafting thousands of original subscribers to become the moderation team.

There are three critical points I want to make about any implementation of this idea.

First, this must be unique to each subverse, rather than sitewide. We're not trying to punish new users, and we already have good limits on the sitewide voting. This system is meant to help each subverse manage their own content. It must be optional - moderators and subscribers are under no obligation to turn it on, and frankly, everything on Voat should always be optional whenever possible to maximize freedom and customization. There is no one size fits all.

Second, the most anyone's vote can weigh is 2 points, to a new user's vote of 1 point. If we want the power to come from the aggregate instead of a clique, then we need to keep the difference in the weights small. If someone has a weight of 10, that's giving them ten times the power of a new user which is very extreme. Maybe we need that when Voat is 10 years old and has 150 million users - we sure as hell aren't there yet, so let's keep it small. Even a small change in weight can have a dramatic effect on content.

Third, we need to see both the total number of votes cast and the total weight of those votes as separate numbers on posts and comments. We don't want to lose sight of how many real people voted on something, and we need to see the weighted total to see if this system is having an effect, and if that effect is positive or negative. This is also to help with transparency.

Seem like reasonable, safe limitations for a starting point?

Now, let's get specific.

Imagine in your mod control panel, you see something like this...

  • user has been subscribed more than [ 360 ] days, add [ 0.2 ] points to vote weight
  • user has acquired more than [ 100 ] SCP from this subverse, add [ 0.3 ] points to vote weight
  • user has acquired more than [ 100 ] CCP from this subverse, add [ 0.4 ] points to vote weight
  • user has acquired more than [ 100 ] CCP from sister subverses [ list ], add [ 0.1 ] points to vote weight

Anything within [ brackets ] in those examples is set by the moderators. If the mods set it so that the total would go higher than 2 points, the weight is still capped at 2 points.

Maybe, someday long down the road when there are a lot more users, we have an option that allows mods to set the max for their sub to 2, or 3, or 4 - but there must always be a sitewide maximum cap no one can pass, and that must be accounted for in the way the ranking algorithm works. The admins will manage that master cap and adjust it as they see fit with community feedback.

The reason to increase the cap a bit over years is so that for large, old subs you could have the original 10k users counting as 3 points, the next 100k users counting as 2 points, and everyone else at 1 point. That would get you a two tier mod team of 110k people which might be what you need for a subverse of one million subscribers. Time will tell, we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

This means each user's vote weights are unique to every single subverse on the site, based on their length of subscribership, level of participation, and quality of content submitted to each subverse. What you earn in one community will not help you in another community - with the exception of that 'sister subverse' feature. I think that's important to have to promote groups of subverses that all form a single community, such as gaming, television, sports, music, images, etc. We need to help those networks form and flourish.

This system also takes the piss out of brigading. The votes of the subscribers of a subverse will count more under this system than the votes of new people just visiting. That means brigades will have duller teeth.

These weights only exist on and only affect posts and comments. Your CCP/SCP is still calculated at one point per person per vote, no weights, exactly as it is now, and I am not in favor of ever changing that. Weights are for helping the ranking algorithms to moderate content and nothing more.

I'd like everyone to chime in, but let's keep the replies constructive. Tell us...

  • do you think this would help solve the moderation problem
  • if you have any fundamental issues with the idea of weighting votes and what worries you about it
  • if you like the proposed implementation or have suggestions for improving it

Full disclosure: I am the top mod of default /r/listentothis, in case the wall of text wasn't giving it away. I know what it takes to grow a community from 100 people to 250k people and a 'default' from 250k to over 3 million - while watching everything slowly slide downhill. We stopped that slide (up to a point), one of the only subs on reddit to pull it off - but the price is too damn high. I think if we'd had a system like this on reddit, the community could have managed itself. That's what I want for Voat.

All this talk of reigning in power moderators avoids a bigger, better question: How do we make moderators (and rules, and bots) unnecessary? I have a proposal to do just that, and build a better Voat.
So, tl;dr is: issues are voted on in sub, different users get different vote weights due to different requirements.
